q: For a body moving along a straight line, which quantity can be positive, negative or zero?
x: Displacement has direction, so along a line it can be positive, negative or zero. Distance, speed and time interval can never be negative.

q: A car drives 8 km due north and then 6 km due south along the same road. The distance covered and the displacement are:
x: Distance adds up the path: 8 + 6 = 14 km. Displacement is the net change in position: 8 − 6 = 2 km, still north of the start.

q: A man walks 12 m due east and then 5 m due south. The magnitude of his displacement from the starting point is:
x: The two walks are at right angles, so displacement = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 m. 17 m is the distance, not the displacement.

q: A particle moves in a plane from the point (1 m, 2 m) to the point (4 m, 6 m). The magnitude of its displacement is:
x: Change in x = 3 m and change in y = 4 m, so displacement = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m. 7 m simply adds the two changes.

q: A particle moves along a circle of radius 5 m and turns through an angle of 60° about the centre. The magnitude of its displacement is (sin 30° = 0.5):
x: The displacement is the chord: 2r sin(60°/2) = 2 × 5 × 0.5 = 5 m. The two radii and the chord form an equilateral triangle. 5π/3 m is the arc length (distance).

q: A stone is thrown straight up, rises 15 m and falls back into the thrower's hand. The distance travelled and the displacement of the stone are:
x: The stone goes 15 m up and 15 m down, so the distance is 30 m. It ends where it started, so the displacement is zero.

q: A body's displacement over a certain time interval is zero. The distance it travelled in that interval:
o: May be zero or greater than zero
x: Zero displacement means the body ended where it started. It may have stayed at rest (zero distance) or gone away and come back (positive distance). Distance is never negative.

q: A car covers 150 m along a straight road in 10 s without changing direction. The magnitude of its average velocity is:
x: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 150 m ÷ 10 s = 15 m s⁻¹. With no change of direction, displacement equals distance.

q: A car travels 40 km due east in 1 h and then 20 km due west in the next 1 h. Its average speed and average velocity for the 2 h are:
o: 30 km h⁻¹ and 30 km h⁻¹ east
30 km h⁻¹ and 10 km h⁻¹ east
10 km h⁻¹ and 10 km h⁻¹ east
x: Average speed = 60 km ÷ 2 h = 30 km h⁻¹. Net displacement = 40 − 20 = 20 km east, so average velocity = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 km h⁻¹ east.

q: A cyclist moving in one direction along a straight road covers the first half of the distance at 20 m s⁻¹ and the second half at 30 m s⁻¹. Her average velocity is:
x: For equal distances, v̄ = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂) = 2 × 20 × 30 ÷ 50 = 24 m s⁻¹. 25 m s⁻¹ would be correct only for equal times.

q: A particle on the x-axis is at x = 2 m at t = 0 and at x = 14 m at t = 4 s. Its average velocity over this interval is:
x: Average velocity = (14 − 2) m ÷ 4 s = 3 m s⁻¹. 3.5 m s⁻¹ wrongly uses the final position 14 m instead of the change in position.

q: A runner goes once along a semicircular track of radius 7 m, from one end of the diameter to the other, in 2 s. Taking π = 22/7, her average speed and the magnitude of her average velocity are:
x: Distance = πr = 22 m, so average speed = 22 ÷ 2 = 11 m s⁻¹. Displacement = diameter = 14 m, so average velocity = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 m s⁻¹.

q: The average velocity of a body over a time interval is zero. This tells us that:
o: It was at rest throughout the interval
Its final position is the same as its initial position
Its average speed was also zero
x: Zero average velocity means zero displacement: the body ended where it began. It may still have moved and accelerated in between, so its average speed need not be zero.

q: The velocity of a body changes uniformly from 6 m s⁻¹ to 14 m s⁻¹ along a straight line. Its average velocity during this change is:
x: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (initial + final) ÷ 2 = (6 + 14) ÷ 2 = 10 m s⁻¹. 8 m s⁻¹ is the change in velocity.

q: Two bodies are shown by straight lines on the same displacement–time graph. The body whose line is steeper has the:
x: The slope of a displacement–time graph is velocity, so the steeper line belongs to the faster body. A straight line means zero acceleration for both.

q: A body moves back towards the origin: its position is 30 m at t = 0 and 0 m at t = 6 s, changing at a steady rate. What velocity does the slope of its displacement–time graph give?
x: Velocity = slope = (0 − 30) ÷ (6 − 0) = −5 m s⁻¹. The negative sign shows the body is moving back towards the origin.

q: The displacement–time lines of two cars on the same road cross each other at one point. At that instant the two cars:
x: Each point on a displacement–time graph gives position at a time, so the crossing point means both cars are at the same place at that instant. Equal velocity would need equal slopes.

q: A ball rolls along a straight floor and gradually comes to rest. Its displacement–time graph is:
o: A curve that gets steeper and steeper
A horizontal line from the start
A curve that gets flatter and finally becomes horizontal
x: The slope of the graph is the velocity. As the ball slows down the slope decreases, and when it stops the graph becomes horizontal.

q: On a displacement–time graph, a body moves from 0 m to 12 m in the first 3 s and then back to 0 m by t = 6 s, both along straight lines. Its average velocity and average speed over 6 s are:
x: Net displacement is zero, so average velocity is zero. Total distance = 12 + 12 = 24 m, so average speed = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 m s⁻¹.

q: At t = 0, car P is at x = 0 moving at a constant 10 m s⁻¹, and car Q is at x = 60 m moving at a constant 5 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. Their displacement–time lines meet at t =
x: P's position is 10t and Q's is 60 + 5t. They meet when 10t = 60 + 5t, so t = 12 s. 6 s wrongly uses P's speed alone (60 ÷ 10).

q: A displacement–time graph can never be a vertical straight line, because that would mean the body has:
x: A vertical line would mean a change of position in zero time, i.e. an infinite slope and so an infinite velocity, which is impossible.

q: The SI unit of acceleration is:
x: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, so its unit is (m s⁻¹) ÷ s = m s⁻². m s⁻¹ is the unit of velocity.

q: A car moving at 8 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² for 4 s. Its velocity at the end of this time is:
x: v = u + at = 8 + 3 × 4 = 20 m s⁻¹. 12 m s⁻¹ is only the gain in velocity, without the initial 8 m s⁻¹.

q: A car's velocity is negative and its acceleration is also negative. The car is:
o: Slowing down in the negative direction
Speeding up in the positive direction
Speeding up in the negative direction
x: When velocity and acceleration have the same sign they point the same way, so the speed increases. Here both point in the negative direction.

q: A train's velocity increases uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 75 m. Its acceleration is:
x: v² = u² + 2as gives 400 = 100 + 2a × 75, so 150a = 300 and a = 2 m s⁻². 4 m s⁻² forgets the factor 2.

q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the time it takes to reach its highest point is:
x: At the top v = 0, so 0 = 20 − 10t and t = 2 s. 4 s is the total time to go up and come back down.

q: A car moving at 30 m s⁻¹ brakes with a uniform deceleration of 5 m s⁻² until it stops. The distance it covers in the last 1 s before stopping is:
x: Run the motion backwards: in the last second the car is like a body starting from rest with a = 5 m s⁻², so s = ½ × 5 × 1² = 2.5 m. 5 m forgets the ½.

q: A ball hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 8 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.1 s. The magnitude of its average acceleration during contact is:
x: Velocity reverses, so the change is 8 − (−10) = 18 m s⁻¹. a = 18 ÷ 0.1 = 180 m s⁻². 20 m s⁻² ignores the change of direction.

q: Variable (non-uniform) acceleration is present when, in equal time intervals, the velocity of a body:
o: Changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time
Changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals of time
x: Variable (non-uniform) acceleration means the rate of change of velocity is not constant, so the velocity changes by different amounts in equal time intervals.

q: Which of the following bodies has a variable acceleration?
o: A stone falling freely in a vacuum
A block sliding down a smooth inclined plane
A car moving at a constant velocity
A skydiver falling through air before reaching terminal velocity
x: As the skydiver speeds up, air resistance grows, so the net force and acceleration keep decreasing. Free fall in a vacuum and a smooth incline give constant acceleration; constant velocity means zero acceleration.

q: For a body moving with uniform acceleration, the acceleration–time graph is:
o: A straight line sloping upward through the origin
x: Uniform acceleration means a has the same value at every instant, so a plotted against t gives a horizontal line.

q: The velocity of a body at t = 0, 1, 2 and 3 s is 0, 2, 6 and 12 m s⁻¹. Its acceleration is:
x: The velocity changes by 2, 4 and 6 m s⁻¹ in successive seconds. The changes are unequal and growing, so the acceleration is variable and increasing.

q: A body starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 4 m s⁻². The distance it covers during the 3rd second alone is:
x: Distance in 3 s = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 m; in 2 s = ½ × 4 × 4 = 8 m. During the 3rd second: 18 − 8 = 10 m.

q: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration along a straight line. Its displacement–time graph is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A curve (part of a parabola) getting steeper with time
A curve getting flatter with time
x: With uniform acceleration from rest, s = ½at², so s against t is a parabola whose slope (velocity) keeps increasing.

q: The acceleration of a train increases steadily from zero as time passes. Its velocity–time graph is:
o: A curve that becomes steeper with time
A curve that becomes flatter with time
x: The slope of a velocity–time graph is acceleration. If acceleration keeps increasing, the slope keeps increasing, so the graph curves upward more and more steeply.

q: Which one of these moves as a projectile?
o: A lift moving up its shaft
A javelin after it leaves the athlete's hand
The blade of a rotating ceiling fan
A car moving along a straight road
x: Once released, the javelin moves forward and falls under gravity at the same time, following a curved path in a vertical plane: projectile motion.

q: A stone thrown horizontally from a roof moves in two dimensions because it:
o: Has acceleration in both the horizontal and vertical directions
Loses horizontal velocity as it falls
Keeps its horizontal velocity while gaining vertical velocity due to gravity
Moves only under its horizontal velocity
x: Gravity acts only vertically, so the stone keeps its horizontal velocity and also gains downward velocity. The two motions together give a curved, two-dimensional path.

q: A ball thrown straight up does NOT move as a two-dimensional projectile because:
o: Gravity does not act on it while rising
Its acceleration changes direction at the top
Its initial velocity has no horizontal component
x: With no horizontal velocity component, the ball moves only along a vertical line, so its motion is one-dimensional.

q: When analysing projectile motion, the axes are usually chosen with:
o: Both axes horizontal and at right angles
The x-axis along the initial velocity and the y-axis perpendicular to it
The x-axis horizontal and the y-axis vertical, origin at the launch point
The y-axis horizontal and the x-axis along the path
x: Choosing x horizontal and y vertical splits the motion into a horizontal part with no acceleration and a vertical part with acceleration g.

q: Ignoring air resistance, which statement about the velocity of a projectile launched at an angle is correct?
o: Its direction changes continuously during the flight
It is constant throughout the flight
Its direction stays the same but its magnitude changes
It is always directed vertically downward
x: The velocity is along the tangent to the curved path, so its direction changes all the time. Its magnitude also changes as the vertical component changes.

q: A dart is thrown horizontally, aimed exactly at the centre of a dartboard. It hits the board a little below the centre because:
o: Its horizontal velocity decreases during the flight
Gravity acts on it only after it slows down
It falls vertically under gravity while it moves horizontally
Its horizontal and vertical velocities cancel
x: During its time of flight the dart accelerates downward at g while moving horizontally, so it drops below the line along which it was aimed.

q: A ball rolls off a horizontal table top at 4 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², after how long will its speed be 5 m s⁻¹?
x: Horizontal component stays 4 m s⁻¹, so the vertical component must be √(25 − 16) = 3 m s⁻¹. t = 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 s.

q: In the absence of air resistance, the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of a projectile during its flight:
o: Becomes zero at the highest point
x: Without air resistance, only gravity does work on the projectile, so kinetic energy and potential energy change into each other while their sum stays constant.

q: Ignoring air resistance, a projectile passes the same height once while rising and once while falling. At these two points its speeds are:
x: With no air resistance mechanical energy is conserved, so at equal heights the kinetic energy, and therefore the speed, is the same.

q: A ball is projected from level ground and lands on the same level after 4 s. Ignoring air resistance, it reached its highest point after:
x: Without air resistance the path is symmetric, so the time to rise equals the time to fall. Time to the top = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 s.

q: A ball's kinetic energy is E when it is launched at 60° to the horizontal. With no air drag, how much kinetic energy does it have at the top of its path? (cos 60° = 0.5)
x: At the top only the horizontal component v cos 60° = v/2 remains. KE = ½m(v/2)² = ¼ × ½mv² = E/4. E/2 forgets to square the factor ½.

q: A 1 kg ball and a 3 kg ball are launched with the same velocity. Ignoring air resistance, their paths are:
o: Different, the heavier ball going less far
Exactly the same, with equal ranges and maximum heights
Different, the heavier ball going higher
Different, the lighter ball landing first
x: Without air resistance both have acceleration g and the same initial velocity, so the motion does not depend on mass and the paths are identical.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the path of a stone thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff is:
x: Horizontal distance grows as t and vertical drop as t², so y is proportional to x²: half of a parabola starting at its highest point.

q: Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of an oblique (angled) projectile's path, its speed is:
x: At the top the vertical component is zero but the horizontal component remains, so the speed is at its minimum value v cos θ, which is not zero.

q: A projectile is launched with speed v at angle θ above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity throughout the flight is:
x: The horizontal component at launch is v cos θ, and with no horizontal force it stays the same for the whole flight. v sin θ is the initial vertical component.

q: A ball is launched at 20√2 m s⁻¹ at 45° above the horizontal (cos 45° = 1/√2). Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity 2 s after launch is:
x: Horizontal component = 20√2 × (1/√2) = 20 m s⁻¹, and it does not change during the flight, so it is still 20 m s⁻¹ after 2 s.

q: An aeroplane flying horizontally at 100 m s⁻¹ at a height of 500 m releases a packet. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the packet travels a horizontal distance before landing of:
x: Time to fall: 500 = ½ × 10 × t², so t = 10 s. The horizontal velocity stays 100 m s⁻¹, so distance = 100 × 10 = 1000 m.

q: 1 s after launch, a projectile's velocity has a horizontal component of 6 m s⁻¹ and a vertical component of 4 m s⁻¹ upward. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal component 2 s after launch is:
x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal component stays 6 m s⁻¹ throughout. Only the vertical component changes.

q: Two balls are thrown horizontally from the top of the same tower with speeds of 5 m s⁻¹ and 10 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, the ratio of their horizontal distances from the tower on landing is:
x: Both fall the same height, so they take the same time. Horizontal distance = speed × time, so the distances are in the ratio 5 : 10 = 1 : 2.

q: Plotting x (horizontal distance travelled) of a projectile against time gives, when air drag is negligible:
o: A straight line through the origin
A curve that becomes flatter with time
x: Horizontal velocity is constant, so x = (v cos θ)t, which is a straight line through the origin with slope v cos θ.

q: If air resistance is NOT ignored, the horizontal component of a projectile's velocity:
o: Becomes zero at the highest point
x: Air resistance acts against the motion and has a backward horizontal part, so the horizontal component falls. It stays constant only when air resistance is ignored.

q: Near the Earth's surface, the acceleration of a projectile (ignoring air resistance) is about:
x: The only force is the projectile's weight, so it accelerates at g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² straight down, like any freely falling body.

q: Over 3 s of flight, by how much does a projectile's vertical velocity change? (g = 10 m s⁻², air drag negligible)
x: The vertical acceleration is 10 m s⁻² downward, so in 3 s the vertical velocity changes by 10 × 3 = 30 m s⁻¹ downward. 45 is the vertical distance a body would fall from rest, not the velocity change.

q: How long after launch does a projectile reach the top of its path if it starts with an upward velocity component of 25 m s⁻¹? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
x: At the top the vertical velocity is zero: 0 = 25 − 10t, so t = 2.5 s. 5 s is the whole time of flight on level ground.

q: From a cliff 45 m high a stone is launched horizontally. How many seconds pass before it lands? (g = 10 m s⁻², air drag negligible)
x: Vertically the stone starts with zero velocity and accelerates at g: 45 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 9 and t = 3 s, whatever its horizontal speed.

q: A stone is thrown horizontally from a cliff top. If its horizontal launch speed is doubled, its time to reach the ground (ignoring air resistance):
x: The time of fall depends only on the vertical motion, which has zero initial velocity and acceleration g in both cases. The horizontal speed changes only how far the stone lands.

q: A ball is fired at 40 m s⁻¹ with a 30° launch angle (sin 30° = 0.5). Three seconds into the flight, what is the vertical part of its velocity? Take g = 10 m s⁻² and neglect air drag.
x: Initial vertical component = 40 × 0.5 = 20 m s⁻¹ upward. After 3 s: 20 − 10 × 3 = −10 m s⁻¹, i.e. 10 m s⁻¹ downward; the ball is already falling.

q: The vertical acceleration of a projectile is the same as that of a freely falling body because:
o: In both cases the only force acting is the body's weight
Air resistance acts upward on both
x: Ignoring air resistance, weight is the only force on each, so each accelerates downward at g. A projectile does have horizontal velocity, but that does not affect its vertical acceleration.

q: At the highest point of an oblique projectile's path, which component of its velocity is zero?
x: At the top the projectile stops rising and is about to fall, so the vertical component is zero. The horizontal component is unchanged.

q: For a projectile, the graphs of horizontal displacement against time and of vertical displacement against time are respectively:
o: A parabola and a straight line
A straight line and a parabola
x: x = (v cos θ)t is linear in t, while y = (v sin θ)t − ½gt² contains t², so its graph is a parabola.

q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 20 m s⁻¹ from a tall tower. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², after 2 s the ratio of its vertical drop to its horizontal distance is:
x: Horizontal distance = 20 × 2 = 40 m. Vertical drop = ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m. Ratio = 20 : 40 = 1 : 2.

q: At the top of its flight, reached 2 s after being launched, a projectile moves at 15 m s⁻¹. What was its speed at launch? (g = 10 m s⁻², no air drag)
x: Horizontal component = 15 m s⁻¹ (the speed at the top). Vertical component at launch = g × 2 = 20 m s⁻¹. Launch speed = √(15² + 20²) = 25 m s⁻¹.

q: Ignoring air resistance, which statement about a projectile launched at an angle is NOT correct?
o: Its vertical acceleration is g downward
Its horizontal velocity decreases as it rises
Its vertical velocity is zero at the highest point
x: The horizontal velocity stays constant, because no horizontal force acts. The other three statements are true.

q: The horizontal range of a projectile equals its horizontal velocity multiplied by its time of flight. The time of flight is decided by:
x: The projectile lands when its vertical displacement returns to zero, which depends only on the vertical component of velocity and g. The horizontal motion then gives the range.

q: A projectile is launched with speed v at angle θ above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal and vertical velocity components at time t are:
o: v cos θ − gt and v sin θ
v sin θ and v cos θ − gt
v cos θ and v sin θ − gt
v cos θ and v sin θ − ½gt²
x: The horizontal component stays v cos θ. The vertical component starts at v sin θ and decreases by g each second: v sin θ − gt. ½gt² belongs to displacement, not velocity.

q: The total time a projectile spends in flight over level ground, for launch speed v at angle θ above the horizontal, is (no air drag):
x: Vertical displacement returns to zero when (v sin θ)t − ½gt² = 0, giving t = 2v sin θ / g. v sin θ / g is only the time to the top, and v² sin 2θ / g is the range.

q: Find the greatest height reached by a ball launched at 20 m s⁻¹, 60° to the horizontal. (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 60° = √3/2, no air drag)
x: H = v² sin²θ / 2g = 400 × (3/4) ÷ 20 = 15 m. 20 m would be the height if it were thrown straight up.

q: How far away does a stone land if fired over level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ and 30° elevation? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 60° = √3/2, no air drag)
x: R = v² sin 2θ / g = 400 × sin 60° ÷ 10 = 40 × √3/2 = 20√3 m (about 34.6 m). 40 m would be the maximum range, at 45°.

q: Two stones are thrown from level ground with equal speeds and land at the same distance. One was launched at 25° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, the other was launched at:
x: Equal ranges at the same speed occur for complementary angles, θ and 90° − θ, because sin 2θ is the same for both. 90° − 25° = 65°.

q: A ball spends 2 s in the air before landing back at launch level. How high did it rise? (g = 10 m s⁻², no air drag)
x: It rises for 1 s, so the initial vertical velocity is 10 m s⁻¹. H = (10)² ÷ (2 × 10) = 5 m, which equals gT²/8.

q: Launch angles of 30° and 60° with equal speed give equal ranges on level ground. How do their flight times compare (30° : 60°)?
x: Time of flight = 2v sin θ / g, so the ratio is sin 30° : sin 60° = ½ : √3/2 = 1 : √3. Their ranges are equal, but their times are not.

q: The launch angle of a projectile on level ground is raised from 45° to 60°, keeping the same speed. Ignoring air resistance, its range and maximum height:
x: Range ∝ sin 2θ, which is greatest at 45°, so the range falls. Maximum height ∝ sin²θ, which keeps rising with θ, so the height increases.

q: A horizontal force of 12 N acts on a 4 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface. The acceleration of the block is:
x: By Newton's second law a = F/m = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m s⁻². 48 m s⁻² multiplies instead of dividing.

q: A 60 kg man stands on a weighing machine in an elevator that is moving upward but slowing down at 2 m s⁻². Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the machine reads:
x: Slowing while moving up means the acceleration is 2 m s⁻² downward. R = m(g − a) = 60 × 8 = 480 N. 720 N would apply if the elevator were speeding up while going up.

q: A rope pulls a 10 kg box across a floor with a horizontal force of 50 N. The friction force on the box is 20 N. The acceleration of the box is:
x: Net force = 50 − 20 = 30 N, so a = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 m s⁻². 5 m s⁻² ignores friction.

q: A raindrop falls at a constant (terminal) velocity. According to Newton's first law, this means that:
o: No force acts on the drop
The air resistance is greater than its weight
The air resistance on the drop is equal to its weight
x: Constant velocity means zero net force, so the upward air resistance exactly balances the downward weight. Both forces still act.

q: A 2 kg mass hangs from a string and is pulled upward with an acceleration of 5 m s⁻². Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the tension in the string is:
x: T − mg = ma, so T = m(g + a) = 2 × 15 = 30 N. 10 N wrongly subtracts the acceleration from g.

q: Blocks of 4 kg and 6 kg are in contact on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 20 N pushes the 4 kg block, which in turn pushes the 6 kg block. The force between the blocks is:
x: Both move together: a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m s⁻². The only horizontal force on the 6 kg block is the contact force, so it is 6 × 2 = 12 N. 8 N is the net force on the 4 kg block.

q: A 5 kg body at rest on a smooth surface is acted on by a constant force of 10 N for 3 s. The distance it covers in this time is:
x: a = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m s⁻², and s = ½at² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 m. 18 m forgets the ½.

q: The SI unit of linear momentum is:
x: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹ (equivalent to N s). kg m s⁻² is the newton, the unit of force.

q: The momentum of a body increases steadily from 10 kg m s⁻¹ to 30 kg m s⁻¹ in 4 s. The net force acting on it is:
x: F = Δp/Δt = (30 − 10) ÷ 4 = 5 N. 10 N wrongly adds the two momenta (10 + 30 = 40) and divides by 4.

q: The velocity of a 2 kg body increases from 3 m s⁻¹ to 8 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. The impulse acting on it is:
x: Impulse = change in momentum = 2 × (8 − 3) = 10 N s. 22 N s adds the two momenta (6 + 16) instead of subtracting.

q: Newton's second law written as F = ma is a special case of F = Δp/Δt. It holds only when:
o: The velocity of the body stays constant
The force acts for a very short time
The mass of the body stays constant
x: F = Δ(mv)/Δt = m(Δv/Δt) = ma only if m does not change. For changing mass, such as a rocket, the momentum form must be used.

q: Cars are built with crumple zones that fold up in a crash. They reduce the force on passengers because they:
o: Increase the time over which the car's momentum changes
Reduce the car's change in momentum to zero
Increase the car's mass during the crash
Reduce the time of the collision
x: For a given change in momentum, F = Δp/Δt, so a longer stopping time means a smaller average force. The change in momentum itself is not reduced.

q: A force on a 2 kg body at rest rises uniformly from zero to 20 N in 0.4 s. Using the area under the force–time graph, the speed of the body after 0.4 s is:
x: Impulse = area of the triangle = ½ × 20 × 0.4 = 4 N s. This equals the change in momentum, so v = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 m s⁻¹. 4 m s⁻¹ forgets the ½.

q: A 0.1 kg ball falling at 20 m s⁻¹ hits the ground and comes to rest without bouncing. The impulse given to the ball by the ground is:
x: Impulse = change in momentum = 0 − (0.1 × 20 downward) = 2 N s upward. The ground pushes up, opposite to the ball's original motion.

q: A swimmer pushes the water backward with her hands and moves forward. This is an example of:
x: The swimmer's push on the water (action) is matched by an equal and opposite push of the water on the swimmer (reaction), which drives her forward.

q: A horse pulls a cart and the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. The horse still moves forward because:
o: The horse's pull on the cart is larger than the cart's pull on the horse
Action and reaction forces cancel each other
The cart's pull acts only after the horse moves
The ground pushes the horse forward with a force larger than the cart's backward pull on it
x: Action and reaction act on different bodies. The forces on the horse are the cart's backward pull and the ground's forward push; the horse accelerates when the ground's push is larger.

q: During a collision, body X exerts force F on body Y, and Y exerts −F on X for the same time. This shows that the total momentum is conserved because:
o: The forces act on the same body and cancel
The impulses on the two bodies are equal and opposite, so their momentum changes cancel
The kinetic energy of each body stays the same
x: Each body receives an impulse F × t, equal in size and opposite in direction, so one gains exactly the momentum the other loses.

q: When a book presses down on a table top, which force forms the third-law partner of this push?
o: Downward pull of the Earth on the table
Upward pull of the book on the Earth
Upward push of the table on the book
x: Action and reaction act between the same two bodies. The book pushes down on the table, so the table pushes up on the book.

q: Two ice skaters at rest on smooth ice push each other apart. Which quantities are equal in magnitude for the two skaters?
o: The forces on them and their changes in momentum
Their speeds and their kinetic energies
x: By the third law the forces are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so the momentum changes are equal. Unequal masses give unequal accelerations, speeds and kinetic energies.

q: Two trolleys of 1 kg and 3 kg are held together with a compressed spring between them and then released. At one instant the 1 kg trolley has an acceleration of 6 m s⁻². At that instant the 3 kg trolley has an acceleration of:
o: 6 m s⁻² in the opposite direction
2 m s⁻² in the opposite direction
18 m s⁻² in the opposite direction
2 m s⁻² in the same direction
x: The spring pushes on both with equal and opposite forces: F = 1 × 6 = 6 N. For the 3 kg trolley a = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m s⁻², in the opposite direction.

q: A book rests on a table. Which pair of forces is NOT an action–reaction pair?
o: The push of the book on the table and the push of the table on the book
The Earth's pull on the book and the book's pull on the Earth
The weight of the book and the upward push of the table on the book
The Earth's pull on the table and the table's pull on the Earth
x: The weight of the book and the table's push both act on the same body (the book); they balance but are not a third-law pair. Third-law pairs act on two different bodies.

q: Momentum and kinetic energy in a perfectly elastic collision (no external force): which are conserved?
o: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
x: Momentum is conserved in every collision without external force. In a perfectly elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved.

q: A 4 kg cart rolling at 5 m s⁻¹ couples with a stationary 6 kg cart, and they move off together. Their common speed is:
x: Momentum before = 4 × 5 = 20 kg m s⁻¹. After: (4 + 6)v = 20, so v = 2 m s⁻¹. 3.3 m s⁻¹ wrongly divides by the 6 kg mass alone.

q: A 10 g bullet moving at 300 m s⁻¹ embeds itself in a 2.99 kg wooden block resting on a smooth surface. The block and bullet move off at:
x: Momentum before = 0.01 × 300 = 3 kg m s⁻¹. Total mass after = 3 kg, so v = 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m s⁻¹.

q: Two identical balls collide head-on and perfectly elastically. Before the collision one moves at 4 m s⁻¹ forward and the other at 2 m s⁻¹ backward. After the collision:
o: The first moves at 2 m s⁻¹ backward and the second at 4 m s⁻¹ forward
Both move forward at 1 m s⁻¹
The first moves at 4 m s⁻¹ backward and the second at 2 m s⁻¹ forward
x: In a head-on elastic collision between equal masses the bodies simply exchange velocities. Check: momentum 4 − 2 = 2 before and −2 + 4 = 2 after.

q: A body of mass m moving at speed v hits an identical body at rest, and the two stick together. The fraction of the original kinetic energy lost is:
x: Common velocity = v/2. KE after = ½(2m)(v/2)² = ¼mv², which is half of the original ½mv². So half the kinetic energy is lost.

q: Which of the following collisions is perfectly elastic?
o: A lump of clay hitting a wall and sticking
A bullet embedding itself in a wooden block
A car crash in which the cars crumple
Collisions between molecules of an ideal gas
x: Kinetic theory treats collisions between ideal gas molecules as perfectly elastic. In the other cases the bodies deform or stick, so kinetic energy is lost.

q: When a bomb initially at rest explodes, the kinetic energy of its fragments comes from:
o: The momentum of the bomb before the explosion
The gravitational pull of the Earth
Nothing, because kinetic energy is conserved
The chemical energy stored in the explosive
x: The bomb starts with zero momentum and zero kinetic energy. The chemical energy of the explosive is changed into kinetic energy, while the total momentum stays zero.

q: A body at rest explodes into exactly two fragments. Just after the explosion the two fragments must move:
o: In opposite directions along the same line
At right angles to each other
With equal speeds whatever their masses
x: Total momentum must stay zero, so the two momenta must be equal and opposite. That needs the fragments to move in exactly opposite directions; their speeds are equal only if their masses are.

q: A shell at rest breaks into two pieces of 3 kg and 2 kg. The 3 kg piece moves off at 4 m s⁻¹. The velocity of the 2 kg piece is:
o: 6 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 3 kg piece
6 m s⁻¹ in the same direction as the 3 kg piece
4 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 3 kg piece
2.7 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 3 kg piece
x: Total momentum stays zero: 3 × 4 = 2 × v, so v = 6 m s⁻¹, in the opposite direction.

q: A 2 kg shell moving at 10 m s⁻¹ explodes into pieces of 1.5 kg and 0.5 kg. The 0.5 kg piece moves backward at 20 m s⁻¹. The velocity of the 1.5 kg piece is:
x: Momentum before = 2 × 10 = 20 kg m s⁻¹. After: 1.5v + 0.5 × (−20) = 20, so 1.5v = 30 and v = 20 m s⁻¹ forward.

q: When a rifle fires a bullet, the bullet gets much more kinetic energy than the rifle because:
o: The bullet gets more momentum than the rifle
The rifle gets no momentum at all
Both get equal momentum, and kinetic energy p²/2m is larger for the smaller mass
Kinetic energy is shared equally between them
x: The rifle and bullet get equal and opposite momenta. Since KE = p²/2m, the bullet with its much smaller mass gets far more kinetic energy.

q: A 50 kg astronaut at rest in space throws a 5 kg toolbox away at 2 m s⁻¹. The astronaut moves off at:
o: 2 m s⁻¹ opposite to the toolbox
20 m s⁻¹ opposite to the toolbox
0.2 m s⁻¹ opposite to the toolbox
0.2 m s⁻¹ in the same direction as the toolbox
x: Total momentum stays zero: 50v = 5 × 2, so v = 0.2 m s⁻¹, in the direction opposite to the toolbox.

q: Two bodies approach each other with a relative speed of 10 m s⁻¹ and collide head-on, perfectly elastically. Their relative speed of separation is:
x: In a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach, so it is 10 m s⁻¹.

q: A light ball moving at 8 m s⁻¹ strikes a heavier ball at rest head-on, perfectly elastically, and bounces straight back at 2 m s⁻¹. The speed of the heavier ball after the collision is:
x: Relative speed of separation = approach = 8 m s⁻¹. Taking forward as positive: v − (−2) = 8, so v = 6 m s⁻¹. 10 m s⁻¹ wrongly treats the rebound as forward.

q: A ball dropped onto a hard floor rebounds to a smaller height than it was dropped from. This shows that the collision with the floor is:
o: Inelastic, with relative speed of separation less than that of approach
Perfectly elastic, with equal relative speeds
Perfectly inelastic, with zero speed of separation
Elastic, with relative speed of separation greater than that of approach
x: A lower rebound means the ball leaves the floor more slowly than it arrived, so kinetic energy is lost and the collision is inelastic. It is not perfectly inelastic, because the ball does bounce.

q: To solve a one-dimensional perfectly elastic collision, the relation u₁ − u₂ = v₂ − v₁ is used together with:
x: The relative-speed relation replaces the kinetic energy equation. Together with m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ it gives two simple equations for the two unknown final velocities.

q: Head-on and perfectly elastic: a 2 kg ball at 3 m s⁻¹ strikes a 1 kg ball that is stationary. What are the velocities of the 2 kg and 1 kg balls just after impact?
o: 1 m s⁻¹ and 4 m s⁻¹ forward
2 m s⁻¹ and 2 m s⁻¹ forward
x: Momentum: 2 × 3 = 2v₁ + v₂, so 2v₁ + v₂ = 6. Relative speed: v₂ − v₁ = 3. Solving gives v₁ = 1 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹, both forward.

q: Ball P moving at 5 m s⁻¹ meets ball Q moving at 3 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. They collide head-on, perfectly elastically, and Q then moves at 4 m s⁻¹ in P's original direction. The velocity of P afterwards is:
o: 4 m s⁻¹ in its original direction
x: Relative speed of approach = 5 + 3 = 8 m s⁻¹, which must equal the speed of separation: 4 − v(P) = 8, so v(P) = −4 m s⁻¹, i.e. 4 m s⁻¹ reversed.
